summary: The genuinely new English preserves the source examples and scientifically important qualifications, but is not yet a stand-alone explanation for an eight-year-old. Abstract terminology, audit-style narration and an actual mid-sentence paragraph split require local English revision. Native structural acceptance and historical Chinese/figure passes are not substantive English approval.

source.scope: Fidelity of the new English to the supplied source text and approvedZh text; not replay of original source extraction or source-image review.
basis: Read all 11 source prose blocks and their 11 English counterparts, with approvedZh as a comparison rather than a recovered approval.
All 13 object kinds, source_refs and source_text values are retained; embedded source.data matches the supplied source lesson.
The faucet, bubble, needle, water-strider, sieve/fabric, dew/rain/rainbow, spacecraft, molecular and rubber examples are retained in order.
No exercise was invented: the source and English both retain zero tasks and one figure.

Modern qualifications replace the source's universal counterfactuals, all-raindrops-as-spheres argument and unqualified rubber analogy rather than silently endorsing them. The English carries the same qualifications as approvedZh.
English errata is empty; no numerical or equation correction is introduced by this English draft.

science.scope: Independent substantive assessment of the bound English claims using the supplied text and stable physics, offline.

checks.conclusion: Growth, neck thinning, separation and fall are qualitatively consistent. Gravity, surface tension and flow are all named. The elastic-film comparison is explicitly temporary; no real elastic bag, foreign shell or tearing material skin is claimed.

The bubble's wall is a liquid film, not solid rubber. Shrinking by air escape is explicitly conditional on continued connection to the straw and an open route for air; the draft does not promise the same result for a sealed bubble.

Support includes the upward component of surface tension, buoyancy and wetting rather than a solid supporting skin. No universal promise that any needle floats is made. The skater comparison does not turn water into ice.
Temporary retention or delayed passage is conditional on holes, material/wetting and pressure. The draft does not assert that all sieves hold water or that all fabrics are waterproof.

Material contact and liquid spreading/sticking are acknowledged. Ink, soap, foam, drizzle and plant water supply are not attributed to surface tension alone. Dewdrop shape remains conditional on the surface it touches.

checks.topic: Gravity, size, free fall and spacecraft
checks.conclusion: Near-spherical shape is limited to a free droplet with small disturbances and sufficiently weak competing deformation. Smaller drops have greater relative surface effects for the same liquid under comparable conditions. Air resistance is not erased by free fall; larger raindrops may deform. Spacecraft liquid is not universally spherical when touching walls or undergoing strong flow.

Refraction, internal reflection and dispersion are included, with a plain-language description of bending, reflection and color separation. Nearly spherical drops aid the familiar rainbow. The draft does not infer universal rainbow impossibility from one nonspherical droplet.

Molecules are not intentional agents and do not all drift inward forever. Molecular motion continues. The surface-area/energy preference is conditional on stable relevant conditions and negligible competing constraints. A sphere minimizes surface area for a given volume. Surface-tension coefficient is distinguished from total force; approximately fixed density is not declared universal. Rubber's changing pull is limited to the relevant elastic range.

The new English prose introduces no two-phase coexistence, phase-equilibrium, melting, boiling, vapor-pressure or fixed-transition-temperature claim. Mentioning a liquid interface does not itself assert two-phase equilibrium.

science.revisionGuardrail: Simplify the English without deleting the outlet/wetting/pressure/contact/flow qualifications or restoring universal original claims. Readability findings do not rescind the above science conclusions for the frozen wording.

readability.method: Manual independent assessment of the actual English text as a stand-alone lesson for an eight-year-old; no readability score or native-output inference.
basis: The opening names surface tension but does not first give a usable positive explanation of what the surface tends to do.
Repeated discussion of what the textbook/original says makes the child track an editorial comparison instead of learning the phenomenon directly.

Wetting and interface receive partial glosses, and the rainbow processes receive a useful plain-language gloss. However, adheres, buoyancy, vertical component, freely suspended, volume, spherical, composition, net force, equilibrium, thermal motion, coefficient, boundary length and incompressibility remain too dense or insufficiently introduced.
Condition lists often substitute for an explanation of what a child would notice or why an effect can stop working.
The final molecular/rubber blocks presuppose several concepts at once. Their caveats are scientifically careful but do not yet form an accessible explanation.

flow.scope: Actual saved English paragraphs, anchors and referent continuity; no rendering or browser evidence.
basis: The 24 flow paragraphs reproduce the draft paragraph sequence exactly, and all five saved boundaries match the draft anchors.
Boundaries at [5, 8, 14, 18, 22] follow sensible conceptual transitions: faucet, other surface examples, drop shapes, molecules and rubber comparison.
Inside the faucet section, paragraph 5 ends with a semicolon and paragraph 6 resumes with lowercase the. This breaks a single drip explanation across paragraphs even though no new section intervenes.
The macro order is usable, but each section needs a concrete observation, explanation and locally attached qualification rather than a succession of editorial cautions.
After author revision, the affected flow paragraphs and before/after anchors must be derived from the new wording; current exact matching cannot approve revised prose.

findings.title: Teach the effect before auditing the original
evidence: surface tension should not always be described as a small force
every consequence listed in the original
The textbook describes a bubble gradually shrinking
findings.problem: A new child reader gets a name and several rebuttals before a positive model. The original and every consequence refer to an unseen text/list. Repeated textbook narration increases this burden, including in the bubble example.
findings.requiredAction: Begin with a short observable effect and a simple conditional model: a liquid surface tends to become smaller, which helps shape small drops. Keep gravity and other causes in the explanation. Replace editorial counterfactuals with direct descriptions. State the bubble-on-a-straw setup and air outlet before explaining shrinking. Retain the scientifically important limitations in short nearby sentences rather than references to an unseen original.
findings.acceptance: A child can explain what surface tension does from the first block and can follow the examples without consulting the original textbook. No universal liquid-behavior or sealed-bubble claim is restored.

findings.title: Introduce everyday terms and figure referents locally
evidence: a dip pen takes ink from an inkwell
a fountain pen stores ink in a sac
how the liquid spreads over and adheres to a material
the narrow neck joining it to the outlet
whose properties should not be equated with those of solid rubber
findings.problem: The partial wetting gloss uses adheres, while pens, sac, pores, outlet and liquid film assume unfamiliar referents. The illustration says Faucet/Attached drop/Detached drop but the prose says tap and never explicitly maps the two drop labels. The bubble sentence uses an abstract properties comparison instead of explaining a thin liquid layer.
findings.requiredAction: Use sticks for adheres, explain wetting through spreading/sticking, and introduce pores as tiny openings. Briefly identify an inkwell as an ink bottle and the historical pen sac as a small ink-holding bag. Identify the outlet as where water leaves the tap, and bridge faucet/tap and attached/still joined versus detached/no longer joined in prose. Describe a bubble wall as a thin liquid layer, not solid rubber. Keep these additions local and do not alter the existing figure or original source records.
findings.acceptance: Every necessary new everyday noun has an immediate plain referent. A child can identify the two drop labels using the English paragraph alone. No new image or source/figure review is needed.

findings.title: Explain support and retention instead of listing conditions
evidence: the vertical component of surface tension, buoyancy, and wetting
Small, light water striders
suitable hole sizes, wetting, and pressure conditions
findings.problem: The reader cannot decode upward support or predict when the examples fail from these technical lists. Water strider is not identified as an insect. Fine-mesh sieve, fibers and pressure conditions introduce several more terms at once.
findings.requiredAction: Explain the upward part of the surface pull and the water's upward push in ordinary words before naming buoyancy. Identify water striders as small insects. Describe a sieve as a mesh with small holes and fibers as the strands of a fabric. Relate the retention qualification to hole size, whether water spreads over the material and how hard the water pushes. Keep carefully placed needle, temporary retention and non-universality explicit; do not add numerical thresholds or guarantee a demonstration.
findings.acceptance: A child can say why the needle can be supported and why some small holes delay water, as well as why neither effect is guaranteed. The wording still includes wetting, pressure and buoyancy rather than a solid-water-skin explanation.

findings.title: Unpack drop shapes, space and rainbow conditions
evidence: For a freely suspended droplet of fixed volume
relative to gravitational deformation
a particular droplet's departure from a sphere
surface effects to dominate the shape
findings.problem: Ball shape, unchanged amount of liquid, no wall contact and competing pushes are encoded in dense technical clauses. The near-weightless gloss and the rainbow's bending/reflection/colors gloss are useful, but the surrounding sentence structure remains too abstract for the target reader.
findings.requiredAction: Introduce spherical as ball-shaped and fixed volume as the same amount of liquid. Explain free suspension as a drop not resting against a solid surface. Separate small-drop behavior, gravity/air effects and wall contact into short sentences. Explain microgravity through the near-weightless setting without saying gravity disappears. Retain the existing light-process gloss and replace the final rainbow logical rebuttal with a direct, qualified description.
findings.acceptance: A child can distinguish a small free drop, dew on a surface, a larger falling raindrop and disturbed/container-contacting space liquid. Refraction, internal reflection and color separation remain; perfect spheres and rainbow impossibility are not asserted.

findings.title: Scaffold the molecular and rubber explanation
evidence: a group of mutually attracting individuals
the same net force in a single direction
temperature, composition, and the adjoining medium
This equilibrium picture
force per unit boundary length
approximate incompressibility
findings.problem: These blocks require molecules, interactions, energy, area, equilibrium, thermal motion and a force-per-length coefficient almost simultaneously. Definitions are replaced by specialist wording and defensive caveats. The exacting final rubber sentence is particularly hard to parse.
findings.requiredAction: Introduce molecules as tiny particles of the liquid, their ongoing motion, surface area as the amount of outside surface, and the extra energy needed to make more surface under the stated stable conditions. Use a simple gathering comparison without intentional molecules. Explain temperature, composition and neighboring material in plain words. For rubber, first contrast less stretching with the liquid coefficient, then explain force for the same length of edge and distinguish that from total force. Explain nearly incompressible as changing volume little when squeezed, while retaining the non-universal density caveat. Replace equilibrium/thermal-motion jargon or gloss it immediately.
findings.acceptance: A child can follow the positive chain from tiny moving particles to surface energy, smaller area and ball shape, then explain why rubber is only an analogy. No permanent inward molecular drift, universal inward force, unqualified fixed density or constant total boundary force is introduced.

findings.title: Keep the drip sentence within a complete paragraph
evidence: A droplet grows and hangs downward;
the narrow neck joining it to the outlet
findings.problem: A blank line follows the semicolon, so the next paragraph begins with a lowercase continuation of the same drip sentence. The exact saved flow reproduces the defect; native anchor resolution is not a readability pass.
findings.requiredAction: Either join the growth/neck/separation sequence into one paragraph or end the growth sentence with a period and start a complete new sentence. Keep the Figure 67 referent with the drip explanation. Update only the affected prose-flow paragraphs and anchor strings from the revised draft; other wording changes may also require their own local anchor updates.
findings.acceptance: No paragraph begins as a lowercase continuation of the previous paragraph's unfinished sentence. The revised flow matches the revised English, and section transitions remain conceptually coherent.
